quizzes.passage:
Finance Commissions have been a regular feature of India's fiscal federalism since 1951, and each one makes recommendations on how tax revenue is shared between the Centre and the States. The sharing takes place through a divisible pool, and the share given to States from that pool is among the most debated figures in public finance.

The debate has several strands. Some have argued that the share is too low for States' needs, and that States have sought a higher share. Others focus on the formula that splits the States' share among the States, since the weights given to different criteria change the amount each State receives.

The concerns about the formula relate to income, demography and economic performance, and to the effect of those factors on particular regions. Some States point to the features that make them distinct, while others want the formula to reward performance more directly.

The discussion also draws on the earlier Commissions, which were appointed in different years and chaired by different persons, so the record of Finance Commissions forms a long series. In each case the report is a formal recommendation to the Government and is placed before Parliament. This makes each report a formal part of the record of Finance Commissions.

quizzes.title: CPI Measures and Their Significance
quizzes.passage: Inflation is an increase in the overall prices of goods and services in an economy over time. Indices are used to measure it, and the Consumer Price Index is one of the most important of them. The index measures the average change over time in the retail prices of goods and services consumed by households, so it follows the prices that ordinary families face in daily life. It also serves as a reference point for comparing prices across different periods. Economic indicators such as GDP and the Index of Industrial Production can be read against this benchmark to observe real changes over time. Every index is built on a base year, which is the reference point against which later prices are compared. Each item in the basket carries a weight that reflects its share of household spending. Over the years, however, the spending of households may drift away from the pattern recorded in that base. When this happens, an index that is not revised risks misrepresenting the actual price rise experienced by households. For this reason, the base of the index needs to be revised from time to time so that its coverage keeps pace with the present shape of consumer demand.

quizzes.title: CPI Targets, Inflation Figures and Uses
quizzes.passage: Prices in an economy rarely stay still. Inflation describes an increase in the overall prices of goods and other items over time, and officials track it through indices. The Consumer Price Index is designed to measure inflation in the retail market, where households buy what they need. It records the average change over time in the retail prices of the items that households consume. Because it follows household purchases, it reflects the cost of living that consumers face. Every index begins with a base year, against which later prices are compared, and the items it covers are chosen to represent typical spending in that period. Spending habits move on, however. When incomes grow and lifestyles change, the purchases of households may shift to new products and new ways of buying. Without periodic revision, an index risks misrepresenting the price rise that households actually experience. Revising the base year allows an index to reflect updated consumption and price structures. Used over time, the index helps observers compare changes in the cost of living from one period to the next. Economic indicators such as GDP and the Index of Industrial Production are also compared with such indices to observe real changes over time.

quizzes.title: CPI and WPI Compared
quizzes.passage: Prices in India are tracked through more than one index, and each index serves a particular purpose. Inflation is an increase in the overall prices in an economy over time, and indices are the standard tool used to measure it. One index measures inflation in the retail market, where households buy items for their own consumption. A second index, the Wholesale Price Index, measures average changes in wholesale prices. The Consumer Price Index reflects the cost of living experienced by consumers. The two indices differ in several respects, so they should not be treated as interchangeable. Each index is linked to a base year, which serves as the reference point for all later comparisons. The coverage of each index is set by the items it includes, and the methods used to build them are not the same. Because the economy changes over time, the structure of each index has to be revised periodically. Economic indicators such as GDP can be compared with these indices over time to observe real changes. Careful reading of the figures helps users understand which measure suits a particular question, whether the focus is household budgets or broader movements in wholesale prices. Index numbers show how prices have moved relative to the base year.
